generated_note: Two properties of the corpus's own stored text that no per-track validator can see. (A) ENCODING DAMAGE: records carrying the signature of Arabic PDF text extraction — reversed lam-alef ligatures and transposed adjacent letters. The issuing bodies published these texts correctly; the damage is in the transcription. Nothing is repaired here, because repair by rule is unsafe: «ال» is itself an Arabic word, both the negative particle and the definite article. (B) THE SAME TEXT UNDER TWO NAMES: pairs of tracks whose text overlaps beyond CONTENT_FLOOR. Overlap alone is not the finding — Saudi practice issues legally DISTINCT instruments from one template, and the eleven cultural-authority licensing regulations are 99% identical while each licenses a different authority. The verdict therefore rests on two facts about the TITLES: whether they name the same subject once the instrument-type words are set aside, and whether they name the same instrument type. A_same_instrument_twice is the case that needs adjudication; B is a law beside its implementing text, which is expected but worth measuring because a reader consulting the regulation should know how much of it restates the law; C is a template family and is correct.
reversed_lam_alef_note: The wider form of the same fault, found by the seed test rather than by a rule: a word form that appears NOWHERE in the tracks with zero sequence signatures, and whose lam-alef swap the corpus uses at least 20 times more often. `real_word_collisions` are the forms that FAILED that test — they do appear in known-good text, because the fault maps real Arabic words onto other real Arabic words («العالقة» the swap of «العلاقة», «عالمة» of «علامة»). Those cannot be classified without reading the sentence, and are listed rather than counted as damage.

stated_limit_of_the_damage_count: The count is a floor, not a total. The seed test classifies a form as damage only when it appears NOWHERE in the tracks with zero sequence signatures — so a damaged form that also leaked into one of those tracks is classified as a real-word collision and is not counted. «الالزمة» is exactly that case: it is damage for «اللازمة», and it occurs six times outside the flagged tracks, so the test cannot call it. Raising the count means reading those sentences, not lowering the threshold — lowering it would sweep in «العالقة» and «عالمة», which are correct Arabic.

why_rule_based_repair_was_rejected.attempt: A repair was designed and measured before being rejected: un-reverse the lam-alef pairs in a damaged word, and accept the result only if it is attested in the corpus's known-good text. On the sequence-signature set it produced a unique attested repair for 658 of 696 word occurrences (95%) with zero ambiguous cases.
why_it_fails: The extraction also SPLITS words. «خ اال المدة» is «خلال المدة» broken in two, and a whole-word repair turns it into «خ الا المدة» — still wrong, but now wrong in a way that no longer carries a damage signature.

The known-good reference is not perfectly clean. «الا» occurs nine times outside the flagged tracks and every one of those is itself damage, so attestation would have certified a wrong form as correct.

Decisively: the fault maps real Arabic words onto other real Arabic words. «العالقة» (suspended, pending) is the swap of «العلاقة» (relationship); «عالمة» (aware) of «علامة» (mark); «صالحية» (fitness) of «صلاحية» (competence). «الشوائب العالقة ببدن السفينة» and «القضايا العالقة لدى المحامين» are correct and say exactly what they mean. No mechanical rule separates damage from correct text in that class; the sentence does.
why_rule_based_repair_was_rejected.conclusion: A partial repair would be worse than disclosed damage: it would leave text that looks repaired, remove the signature that flags it, and make the disclosure's own count untrue. The text is left as published-and-damaged, and the disclosure now carries the reason.
